Decisions taken by the Governing Council of the ECB (in addition to decisions setting interest rates)
November 2026
27 November 2026
External communication
Agreement for Sweden to join T2
On 25 November 2026 the ECB announced that it had concluded an agreement with Sveriges Riksbank for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. More information is available in the press release issued at the occasion of the signing ceremony with ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen of the T2 currency participation agreement.
Market operations and market infrastructure and payments
Acceptance of marketable assets issued on distributed ledger technology (DLT) platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime as Eurosystem collateral
On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the acceptance of marketable assets issued on DLT platforms licensed under the EU DLT Pilot Regime Regulation (EU) 2022/858 and reachable via TARGET2-Securities (T2S) as eligible collateral for Eurosystem credit operations, subject to specific Eurosystem requirements. This decision is part of a roadmap exploring ways to expand eligibility to assets issued and settled entirely on DLT networks. The decision is due to take effect in June 2027 and is explained in a press release available on the ECB’s website. It follows the ECB announcement of 27 January 2026 that marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using DLT will be accepted as collateral. These decisions testify to the Eurosystem’s commitment to aligning its collateral framework with advances in technology, while upholding the principles of adequacy of collateral, safety, efficiency and a level-playing field.
Macroprudential policy and financial stability
Financial Stability Review – November 2026
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council held an exchange of views on the basis of the November 2026 edition of the Financial Stability Review and authorised its publication on the ECB’s website. In addition to providing an overview of key financial stability vulnerabilities in the euro area, this edition includes three special features. The first discusses the financial stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy and the financial industry. The second explores the complex interplay between AI and cybersecurity. The third assesses the financial stability implications of large initial public offerings and equity issuance in general, as well as how they both interact with the trend towards passive investing. The Financial Stability Review was published on 18 November 2026 on the ECB’s website, together with a related press release.
Banknotes and coins
2026 study on payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area 
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council took note of the results of the 2026 study on the payment attitudes of consumers in the euro area and approved its publication on the ECB’s website. The results show that consumers are increasingly using digital means of payment, while cash continues to play an important role. Moreover, while payment practices are changing, consumers’ own preferences nonetheless remain stable. The results of the study, together with a related press release, are available on the ECB’s website. 
Advice on legislation
ECB Opinion on the supervisory independence of the Bank of Greece and prevention of conflicts of interest of its members of staff and governance body
On 4 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/33 at the request of the Greek Ministry of Economy and Finance.
ECB Opinion on designating the Deutsche Bundesbank as a recipient of administrative data for statistical purposes
On 10 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/34 at the request of the Deutsche Bundesbank on behalf of the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy.
ECB Opinion on the competences of the Supervisory Board of the Magyar Nemzeti Bank
On 19 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/35 at the request of the Hungarian Ministry of Finance.
ECB Opinion on a tax on excess profits of credit institutions and other specified companies
On 25 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/36 at the request of the Bulgarian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance. 
Corporate governance
ECB Recommendation on the external auditors of the Bank of Greece
On 5 November 2026 the Governing Council adopted Recommendation ECB/2026/29 to the Council of the European Union on the external auditors of the Bank of Greece.
International and European cooperation
Eurosystem participation in Phase II of Project Agorá
On 18 November 2026 the Governing Council approved the participation of the Eurosystem – represented by the Banque de France – in Phase II of the BIS Innovation Hub’s Project Agorá which is due to run until December 2027. This ongoing Eurosystem participation in Agorá is without prejudice to any future policy decisions the Eurosystem may take on the possibility of providing central bank money on external or shared DLT platforms. At the invitation of the Banque de France and the ECB, other interested Eurosystem national central banks may join a newly established Eurosystem technical group to operationalise this participation in Project Agorá Phase II.
ECB Banking Supervision
Disclosure of Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) methodologies
On 3 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish: the SREP 2026 methodology applied to significant institutions under the direct supervision of the ECB, the more detailed SREP methodology for operational risk and ICT risk, the more detailed SREP methodology for assessing capital adequacy, and the internal governance and risk management SREP methodology. The related press release, together with these four documents, is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website. 
Results of the SREP 2026 exercise
On 9 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the SREP 2026 aggregated results. Overall, these results show that the euro area banking sector has continued to be resilient in the face of the heightened uncertainty clouding the economic and geopolitical environment. The publication is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website. 
Outcome of the 2026 risks and priorities exercise
On 12 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish the outcome of the 2026 risks and priorities exercise, listing the supervisory priorities for the next three years (2027-29). The publication is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website. 
2027 Supervisory Examination Programme (SEP) for on-site inspections and internal model investigations at significant institutions
On 16 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board concerning the 2027 SEP for on-site inspections and internal model investigations at significant institutions under European banking supervision. The on-site SEP is based on the SSM supervisory priorities for 2027-29 published on the ECB’s banking supervision website.
Less significant institution (LSI) supervision report 2026
On 23 November 2026 the Governing Council did not object to a proposal by the Supervisory Board to publish a report on the supervision of LSIs in 2026. The report, which examines the structural features of the LSI sector, its key developments and major supervisory activities, is available on the ECB’s banking supervision website.

PRESS RELEASE
ECB Consumer Expectations Survey results – October 2026
27 November 2026
Compared with September 2026:
median consumer perceptions of inflation over the past 12 months and expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased significantly, while median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased slightly and those for five years ahead were unchanged;
expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months declined, while expectations for spending growth over the next 12 months were unchanged;
expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased, while the expected unemployment rate in 12 months’ time decreased;
expectations for growth in the price of homes over the next 12 months decreased, while expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged.
Inflation
In October the median rate of perceived inflation over the previous 12 months increased to 4.1% from 3.6% in September and stood at its highest level since July 2024. Median expectations for inflation over the next 12 months also rose to 3.5% from 3.1%, but remained below the level reached at the start of the conflict in March 2026 (4.0%). Median expectations for inflation three years ahead increased to 3.0% from 2.9%, returning to the March 2026 level. Median expectations for inflation five years ahead were unchanged at 2.5% for the third consecutive month, the highest level since the start of the series in August 2022. Uncertainty about expectations for inflation over the next 12 months increased for the second consecutive month, remaining higher than the level prior to the start of the conflict in the Middle East. Respondents in the bottom income quintile continued to report higher inflation perceptions and expectations, on average, than those in the top quintile. Younger respondents (aged 18-34) continued to report lower inflation perceptions and expectations than older respondents (aged 35-54 and 55-70).
Inflation results
Income and consumption
Consumers’ expectations for nominal income growth over the next 12 months fell to 0.6% from 1.1% in September. While expectations declined across all income quintiles, the decline was most pronounced in the bottom income quintile (by 0.7 percentage points to 0.8%) and in the top quintile (by 0.8 percentage points to 0.4%). Perceived nominal spending growth over the previous 12 months increased to 5.4% from 5.3% in September, while expected nominal spending growth over the next 12 months was unchanged at 3.7%.
Income and consumption results
Economic growth and labour market
Expectations for economic growth over the next 12 months increased in October to -1.3% from -1.5% in September. Expectations for the unemployment rate 12 months ahead decreased to 11.0% from 11.3% in September. As observed in previous months, households in the bottom income quintile expected the highest unemployment rate 12 months ahead (13.3%), while households in the top income quintile expected the lowest rate (9.5%). Consumers continued to expect the future unemployment rate to be only slightly higher than the perceived current unemployment rate (10.4%), suggesting a broadly stable labour market outlook. Quarterly data revealed a somewhat mixed labour market sentiment. Unemployed respondents reported a lower expected probability of finding a job over the next three months, at 29.6% in October compared with 30.8% in July. Employed respondents reported a lower expected probability of job loss over the next three months, at 9.4% in October compared with 9.8% in July.
Economic growth and labour market results
Housing and credit access
Consumers expected the price of their home to increase by 3.3% over the next 12 months, lower than in September (3.5%). As in previous months expectations for home price growth over the next 12 months remained, on average, higher in the lowest income quintile (3.8%) than in the highest income quintile (3.0%). Expectations for mortgage interest rates in 12 months’ time remained unchanged from July, at 4.9%. As in previous months, households in the top income quintile expected the lowest mortgage interest rates 12 months ahead (4.6%), while those in the bottom quintile expected the highest rates (5.4%). The net percentage of households reporting a tightening (relative to those reporting an easing) of access to credit over the previous 12 months increased compared with September. The net percentage of households expecting tighter credit conditions over the next 12 months (relative to those expecting an easing) also increased compared with September, reaching its highest value since October 2023. Quarterly data showed that the share of consumers who reported having applied for credit during the past three months increased slightly to 14.4% in October, from 14.3% in July.
Housing and credit access results
The release of the Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) results for November is scheduled for 7 January 2027.
For media queries, please contact: Benoit Deeg, tel.: +49 172 1683704.
Notes
The fieldwork for the latest CES wave was carried out between 1 October and 2 November 2026.
The main aggregate results for individual countries and the euro area are published on the ECB Data Portal and on the ECB’s website every month. 
Unless otherwise indicated, the statistics presented in this press release refer to the 2% winsorised mean. For further details, see ECB Consumer Expectations Survey – Guide to the computation of aggregate statistics.
The CES is a monthly online survey of, currently, around 19,000 adult consumers (i.e. aged 18 or over) from 11 euro area countries: Belgium, Germany, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal and Finland. The results are used for policy analysis and complement other data sources used by the ECB.
Further information about the survey and the data collected is available on the CES web page. Detailed information can also be found in the following two publications: Bańkowska, K. et al., “ECB Consumer Expectations Survey: an overview and first evaluation”, Occasional Paper Series, No 287, ECB, Frankfurt am Main, December 2021; and Georgarakos, D. and Kenny, G., “Household spending and fiscal support during the COVID-19 pandemic: Insights from a new consumer survey”, Journal of Monetary Economics, Vol. 129, Supplement, July 2022, pp. S1-S14.
The survey results do not represent the views of the ECB’s decision-making bodies or staff.

Payments systems Memorandum of Understanding 
 Bank of England, PRA, FCA and PSR review Memorandum of Understanding in relation to payment systems in the UK 
 Published on 
 26 November 2026 
Authorities complete 2026 review of Payments Memorandum of Understanding
The Bank of England (the Bank), Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Payment Systems Regulator (PSR) have completed their annual review of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on payments.
The Authorities have considered the effectiveness and efficiency of their coordination under the MoU. This includes feedback from industry and regulated firms to determine whether the MoU’s principles of coordination and cooperation continue to be met in practice.
The review found that cooperation and coordination remain effective, with respondents welcoming tangible progress in how the Authorities work together. Examples of this include collaborating on a range of developments, including the future regime for dual regulated stablecoin issuers and other innovations in payments, including the work of the Payments Vision Delivery Committee.
Following the review, the Authorities have concluded that no changes to the MoU are needed at this time.
The Authorities have provided further updates to the information detailing each Authority’s regulatory remit and will continue working together to identify areas where greater coordination would benefit the industry.
This will help firms navigate the regulatory landscape and support a more coordinated and effective approach to payments regulation. This approach is further embedded through the Government’s decision to consolidate the PSR into the FCA, meaning greater coordination, clearer responsibilities and a simpler experience for firms.

Statistical Notice 2026/09 - Update to the classification of accounts guide 
 Statistical Notices update the definitions and guidance contained in the Banking Statistics Yellow Folder 
 Published on 
 26 November 2026 
Statistical Notice 2026/09 
Background
The Bank of England has updated the Classification of Accounts Guide (CAG) to provide additional clarity on the classification of non-resident counterparties for statistical reporting purposes.
The changes bring together guidance that is currently set out across the CAG and the Form CC/CL frequently asked questions. They are intended to improve the clarity and consistency of the published guidance and do not introduce new statistical reporting requirements. 
Changes to the Classification of Accounts Guide
The Bank has updated its CAG on the following:
Look-through approach for non-resident counterparties: as previously detailed in the Form CC/CL FAQs, the CAG has been clarified to explain that the look-through approach does not apply to non-resident counterparties in the same way as it applies to UK-resident counterparties.
EU non-resident Deposit-taking Corporations: the guidance on the use of the European Central Bank’s published list has been clarified. An entity identified as a credit union on that list should be classified as a non-resident deposit-taking corporation.
Sovereign wealth funds: sovereign wealth funds have been added to the examples of counterparties that should be classified as non-resident other financial corporations.
Minor housekeeping changes: Minor changes have been made to improve the readability of the CAG. 
Reporting Implications
These amendments clarify the Bank’s existing statistical reporting guidance. They do not introduce new data requirements or changes to reporting forms.
Reporting institutions should review the updated CAG, and ensure that the clarified guidance is reflected in their own classification of counterparties when completing relevant statistical returns.
The updated guide applies from 26 November 2026 on November-2026 data.
Further information
The updated Classification of Accounts Guide is available on the Bank of England’s statistical reporting webpage. Any queries concerning this notice should be directed to the Money and Credit Group by emailing DSDMCG@bankofengland.co.uk.
Footnote
A summary of all Statistical Notice items that are yet to come into effect are also available to view on the Statistical notices page. Statistical Notices should be received by all those responsible for the completion of Bank of England returns. To amend the circulation list please subscribe.

Meeting of 28-29 October 2026
Account of the monetary policy meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank held in Frankfurt am Main on Wednesday and Thursday, 28-29 October 2026
26 November 2026
1. Review of financial, economic and monetary developments and policy options
Financial market developments
Ms Schnabel started her presentation on the latest financial market developments with the observation that higher energy prices since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 September 2026 had reinforced concerns about persistent inflationary pressures. At the same time, market attention had shifted towards fiscal dynamics and concerns about the increasingly debt-financed artificial intelligence (AI) investment cycle. 
Energy price pressures had intensified substantially since the September meeting, pushing oil and gas prices above the adverse scenario of the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In response to renewed tensions in the Middle East, the latest oil futures curve had shifted markedly higher compared with the baseline of the September projections and had also moved visibly above the adverse scenario over the short term. The repricing in gas markets had been even more pronounced, with the futures curve currently standing well above the adverse scenario over the entire horizon. 
Diesel refining margins stood at a historically high level, with euro area diesel crack spreads – the differences between wholesale prices and crude oil prices – above the levels observed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Freight rates from the Gulf region to Europe had surged to record highs, while the probability of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 was at its lowest since the start of the war in the Middle East. The increase in energy prices was reflected in inflation compensation. Inflation fixings throughout 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and remaining above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028, while inflation fixings for 2028 were broadly unchanged. Option-implied inflation risks continued to be skewed to the upside over the next two years and five years. 
Despite the sharp increase in energy prices and the deterioration in the inflation outlook, expectations for the key ECB interest rates stood near their September levels. The one-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate one year ahead had decoupled from energy prices, consistent with communication that interest rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Immediately after the Governing Council’s September monetary policy meeting, the OIS forward curve had shifted markedly higher, temporarily pricing in more than four additional 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months, before investors pared back expectations to just under three additional hikes. Market pricing adjusted for term premia pointed to an expected peak in the deposit facility rate at around 3%, implying a more pronounced tightening than the median expectation of participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts, which foresaw only one more hike. 
Euro area risk-free rates had stabilised and, at longer tenors, had even declined since the September meeting, while US rates had risen across maturities on the back of higher real rates. The divergence between real yields in the euro area and the United States was consistent with investors’ perceptions of a more dynamic US economy.
The rise in euro area ten-year rates relative to the average in 2024 had been driven primarily by higher real term premia, reflecting increased uncertainty about the long-run macroeconomic outlook and a growing net supply of public and private debt. Higher expected short-term real rates and higher inflation expectations accounted for around one-third of the increase in ten-year rates. Moreover, the shift in stock-bond correlations into positive territory pointed to reduced diversification benefits from bonds amid more frequent adverse supply shocks, requiring greater compensation to hold duration risk.
As higher real rates raised governments’ borrowing costs and reduced fiscal space, sovereign bond yields had become more sensitive to differences in the fiscal outlook. Sovereign bond spreads had increased notably for some countries since the previous monetary policy meeting, but they had generally remained well below earlier peaks and broadly in line with fundamentals. A greater responsiveness of euro area sovereign bond yields to market stress also reflected a shift towards more price-sensitive investors. Despite the recent widening in spreads, systemic stress indicators had remained contained, well below levels recorded in previous episodes of market strain. 
Euro area bank equities had overall remained resilient and, despite a recent correction, had continued to trade in positive territory over the year to date, benefiting from the higher interest rate environment and banks’ solid profitability and strong capital positions. Euro area banks had continued to reduce their domestic exposures in total government bond holdings. This suggested that they were less exposed to domestic shocks, as portfolios had become more diversified.
Concerns about inflation, financial conditions and fiscal policy had also extended to broader equity markets, with euro area stocks underperforming. A further factor weighing on equity markets globally had been the sharp correction in tech stocks, as growing concerns about the increased debt financing of the AI build-out and the returns it would generate had caused significant volatility. The substantial increase in debt issuance by hyperscalers to finance AI investment had so far been smoothly absorbed in euro area corporate bond markets, but at a higher cost for issuers. 
Weakening risk sentiment towards the euro area and diverging interest rates had been reflected in the EUR/USD exchange rate, which had depreciated noticeably since the September meeting. Overall, financial conditions had tightened recently, mainly owing to a correction in risk assets and higher sovereign yields, although partly offset by the weakening of the exchange rate. 
Ms Schnabel then turned to short-term funding markets. Bank borrowing costs in overnight repo markets had continued their gradual upward trend, with the spreads between rates for French, Italian and Spanish collateral broadly stable against those using German collateral. Liquidity redistribution across banks had continued to operate smoothly, with money market conditions adjusting well to an environment with less excess liquidity. On 27 October 2026, recourse to the Eurosystem’s standard refinancing operations had risen to its highest level since the end of 2016, with short-term money market rates remaining close to the deposit facility rate. Both the seven-day main refinancing operation, which covered the October 2026 month-end, and the three-month longer-term refinancing operation, which covered the 2026 year-end, had contributed to the increase. Overall, this was a comforting sign that banks were becoming more accustomed to using standard refinancing operations in their day-to-day liquidity management as balance sheet normalisation and the reduction of excess liquidity progressed.
The global environment and economic and monetary developments in the euro area
Mr Lane then went through the latest economic, monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area.
Starting with inflation in the euro area, Mr Lane noted that headline inflation, as measured by the Harmonised index of Consumer Prices (HICP), had risen to 3.8% in September, from 3.2% in August. This increase had been driven by energy price inflation, which had increased markedly to 18.9% from 14.3%. Diesel and petrol prices had reached new peaks in September, in part reflecting elevated refining margins. Inflation excluding energy had risen to 2.3% in September, from 2.1% in August. Food inflation had increased by 0.2 percentage points in September, to 1.3%, in part owing to the impact of the summer heatwaves on the unprocessed food component. Core inflation (HICP inflation excluding energy and food) had edged up to 2.5% in September, from 2.4% in August: a 0.1 percentage point decline in goods inflation to 1.1% had been offset by a 0.2 percentage point increase in services inflation to 3.2%. 
The pass-through of the energy shock to inflation remained most visible in direct effects. Indirect effects had, overall, evolved as expected and were still limited. So far there had been no material signs of second-round effects. Indicators of underlying inflation had remained broadly stable and wage pressures remained moderate. Compensation per employee had grown by 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% in the first quarter, while rising productivity had helped contain the growth of unit labour costs. At the same time, the early stages of the pricing chain pointed to upward pressures. The ECB’s forward-looking wage tracker suggested that negotiated wage growth would fluctuate between 2.5% and 2.8% in the remaining months of 2026 and average 2.6% in the first three quarters of 2027, broadly in line with the September staff projections. However, in the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) input prices had picked up to 67.3 in October, from 67.0 in September and 62.8 in August. In addition, the selling price expectations of firms over the coming year had increased in the latest round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area. These signals suggested that indirect and second-round effects would become more material over time, as anticipated in the September staff projections.
Market and survey-based inflation expectations over shorter horizons had risen, but most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stood at around 2%, supporting the stabilisation of inflation around target in the medium term. Estimates of market-implied inflation expectations (derived from measures of inflation compensation by adjusting for risk premia) averaged 3.1% for 2026, 3.3% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028. Expectations of professional forecasters for headline inflation had been revised up for 2027 but were unrevised for 2028 at 2.0%. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations of consumers were broadly stable, as were expectations of firms, according to the second quarter and third quarter rounds of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises. 
Brent crude oil prices (front month – based on futures) had increased by 13% to USD 115 per barrel since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting, in an environment of heightened volatility, elevated freight rates and high global prices for refined products. Price pressures had been particularly pronounced for physical Brent contracts, which reflected prices for more immediate delivery than the front-month prices. Gas prices had increased by 22% to €97 per MWh over the same period, owing to upward pressure from the Middle East conflict. The euro had depreciated by 4.0% against the US dollar since the September meeting, and by 2.2% in nominal effective terms. 
The incoming information pointed to continued global economic growth in the third quarter, with the global composite output PMI (excluding the euro area) increasing to 54.5 in September, reflecting expansion in both the manufacturing and services sectors. At the same time, stocks of finished goods had increased to well above their long-term averages, suggesting some hoarding of finished goods to insulate against persis

Record of the Financial Policy Committee meeting on 19 November 2026
Headline judgements and policy actions
Overall summary
Since the July Financial Stability Report (FSR), the conflict in the Middle East has continued to disrupt global energy markets and supply chains; concerns about sovereign debt sustainability have intensified; and there have been repeated swings in investors’ expectations about the future earnings of artificial intelligence (AI) companies. These developments have contributed to higher expected policy rates, higher bond yields and volatility in financial markets. Some market moves have been amplified by vulnerabilities previously identified by the Financial Policy Committee (FPC).
Despite some amplification within markets, spillovers across markets have been limited and the UK financial system has been resilient. AI investment has supported global growth. However, the very rapid expansion and broadening of its financing – in a form that is increasingly complex, circular and opaque – is also contributing to a deepening of interconnections across the global financial system, making it increasingly likely for stress in one area to propagate to another. Alongside this, the higher interest rate and cost environment is eroding financial headroom for some households and adding to sovereign debt sustainability pressures. Taken together, these developments heighten the risk that multiple vulnerabilities crystallise simultaneously. 
Meanwhile, frontier AI capabilities have continued to grow since the July FSR, notably in the sophistication of AI agents and open-weight AI models. Recent incidents have further illustrated the challenges in aligning and controlling both individual agents and multi-agent dynamics. These developments are making cyber and operational risks a more prominent threat to financial stability, and are contributing to deeper interconnections across the financial system through common technologies and providers.
Global risk environment
The continued conflict in the Middle East has led to a protracted negative supply shock to the global economy. Energy prices have increased since the July FSR, adding to inflationary pressures and contributing to higher interest rates. The outlook for inflation and interest rates remains uncertain and sensitive to developments in the Middle East and their impacts.
Global growth has so far been resilient, in part supported by AI-related investment. This investment also increases the demand for capital which may be contributing to upward pressure on global real interest rates. Uncertainty over the pace of data-centre development, and how much AI investment will translate into future earnings, has contributed to asset price volatility.
Financial vulnerabilities
Vulnerabilities previously highlighted by the FPC in sovereign debt markets, risky asset valuations, and risky credit markets including private credit, remain and, in some cases, have amplified market volatility.
Sovereign debt-to-GDP ratios continue to move upwards globally, reducing the capacity of governments to respond to future shocks. Government bond yields have risen further, reaching near two-decade highs in several advanced economies. In the UK, the increase in yields has mainly reflected higher expected policy rates, driven by higher energy prices and resilient growth, rather than higher term premia. Fiscal and political uncertainty have contributed more materially to increases in yields in some other countries, particularly France. Many sovereign bond markets are characterised by a relatively high use of leverage by hedge funds pursuing similar trading strategies across jurisdictions. Market intelligence suggests that deleveraging by hedge funds contributed to the increase in French sovereign bond yields. Spillovers from French sovereign bonds to other markets, including gilts, have been limited.
UK gilt and gilt repo markets have functioned well, with gilt bid-offer spreads remaining within historical norms. Hedge fund leverage remains elevated by historical standards, although net repo borrowing has declined somewhat since July. In a severe stress, deleveraging by highly leveraged market participants could amplify market moves, impair market functioning and transmit stress back to banks providing financing to these participants. Although the gilt repo market has been resilient recently, past episodes of market dysfunction have highlighted the importance of reforms to ensure the resilience of this market in stress (see Box A of the FSR).
Equity valuations remain stretched on some measures, despite recent falls, with valuations of AI and technology-related companies embedding strong expectations for future earnings. Leveraged funds and retail investors remain exposed to AI stocks, with hedge funds also obtaining leverage through significant prime brokerage borrowing. The value of AI-related equities fell sharply following the US midterm elections, as investors re-assessed the scale, pace and cost of AI-related investment. These moves were amplified by some hedge funds deleveraging. Recent volatility in South Korean equity markets has also provided evidence that procyclical rebalancing by leveraged exchange-traded funds can amplify falls in equity prices. While spillovers to other markets were limited across these episodes, in a more severe shock, losses on equity positions could also lead globally active investors to deleverage in other markets, including sovereign debt markets.
Higher borrowing costs have increased refinancing pressures in corporate debt markets, particularly for weaker borrowers. Spreads widened sharply for US CCC-rated debt and for some lower-quality AI-related borrowers. Spread widening across higher-rated corporate debt has been more limited. There are some signs of increasing stress in parts of private credit, though vulnerabilities have not materially changed overall and stress remains more contained among UK borrowers. A further tightening in risky credit markets could increase financing costs for UK businesses and amplify the impact of an adverse shock.
AI-related financing has grown rapidly and is increasingly spanning equity markets, public bond markets, private credit and more complex financing structures. This is increasing interconnections across the financial system, making it more likely for stress in one area to propagate to another. Hyperscaler bond issuance is set to exceed $305 billion in 2026, accounting for around 8% of global investment grade issuance, with the share rising considerably when considering the broader AI-related issuer ecosystem. Some AI-related companies are also providing finance to others in the sector to support investment, in arrangements linked to future revenue commitments, strengthening sectoral interconnections. Greater use of debt financing could increase the potential for losses in the financial system, while more complex structures and circular financing arrangements can make it more difficult to identify concentrations of risk and where exposures ultimately sit.
Operational vulnerabilities
Firms will need to keep pace with the growing scale and sophistication of cyber threats, including by ensuring that any deployment of frontier AI to identify and remediate cyber threats is undertaken safely, while accelerating long-term preparations for quantum-resistant cryptography. They will also need credible arrangements to recover quickly from operational disruption, in order to maintain the provision of vital financial services. Taken together, these will place competing demands on technology skills and management capacity. A failure to take action will compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications.
Frontier AI capabilities have continued to grow since the July FSR, notably in the sophistication of AI agents and open-weight AI models. Recent incidents have further illustrated the challenges in controlling the risk that increasingly autonomous AI agents act in ways that are misaligned with the objectives intended by developers and users. Separately, the rapid development of open-weight AI models that could be run more cheaply than proprietary models, with safeguards more easily disabled or removed, can make advanced AI models more readily available and useful to malicious actors.
In addition, recent Google Cloud and Microsoft outages have illustrated how operational dependencies mean disruption at a single provider can affect many firms at once. Firms increasingly rely on common technologies and third-party providers, and growing AI adoption deepens these dependencies and creates new ones. This underlines the importance of continuing to operationalise the UK’s critical third party (CTP) regime.
The FPC underlines the importance of firms engaging with guidance from regulatory authorities, such as the joint consultation paper published on 19 November by the Bank, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority on Cyber Risk and Resilience Management, with proposals for a set of principles-based and outcomes-focused expectations for regulated firms and FMIs to strengthen their cyber risk and resilience. The FPC also notes the importance of sector-wide collaboration in helping firms address emerging frontier AI risks and ensuring the system continues to deliver vital financial services throughout operational incidents.
Further ahead, quantum computing could compromise widely used cryptography and hence cyber security. This makes an orderly transition to quantum-resistant cryptography a priority and has implications for actions and decisions firms have to take now.
Overall, the FPC judges that the evolving operational risk environment reinforces the need for significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience.
UK household, corporate and banking system resilience
UK household and corporate balance sheets remain strong in aggregate, supported by stronger than expected GDP growth, but financial headroom is being eroded across borrowers, with some households more affected than others. Successive interest-rate and cost shocks are reducing the capacity of some households to absorb further shocks. Businesses are facing higher costs and tighter financial conditions. Pressures are greatest for small and medium-sized enterprises, energy-intensive firms and highly leveraged corporates, particularly where exposure to higher energy costs, limited financial buffers and refinancing needs overlap.
The UK banking system remains well capitalised with high levels of liquidity, and impairments remain low. The banking system therefore has the capacity to support households and businesses even if economic and financial conditions were to be substantially worse than expected. Despite heightened uncertainty, banks have continued to support lending to the real economy – aggregate gross lending to UK households and businesses in 2026 Q3 was 9% higher

Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement 
On November 24, 2026, NXP B.V., NXP Funding LLC, NXP USA, Inc. (the “Issuers”) and NXP Semiconductors N.V. (the “Company”) completed an underwritten public offering of €500,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 4.625% Senior Notes due 2034 (the “2034 Notes”) and €500,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 4.875% Senior Notes due 2037 (the “2037 Notes” and, collectively with the 2034 Notes, the “Notes”). The Notes were offered and sold pursuant to the Issuers’ and the Company’s automatic shelf registration statement on Form S-3ASR (Registration No. 333-289512), which was filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) and became effective on August 12, 2025. 
The Company and the Issuers intend to use the net proceeds from the offering of the Notes for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures or debt repurchases or repayments. 
The Notes were issued pursuant to an indenture, dated as of May 16, 2022 (the “Base Indenture”), among the Issuers, the Company, as guarantor, and Deutsche Bank Trust Company Americas, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by the third supplemental indenture, dated as of November 24, 2026, among the Issuers, the Company, as guarantor, and the Trustee (the “Third Supplemental Indenture” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”). Interest is payable on the 2034 Notes annually in arrears at an annual rate of 4.625% on February 24 of each year, beginning on February 24, 2027. The 2034 Notes will mature on February 24, 2034. Interest is payable on the 2037 Notes annually in arrears at an annual rate of 4.875% on November 24 of each year, beginning on November 24, 2027. The 2027 Notes will mature on November 24, 2037. 
At any time prior to (i) November 24, 2033 (the date three months prior to the maturity date of the 2034 Notes) for the 2034 Notes and (ii) August 24, 2037 (the date three months prior to the maturity date of the 2037 Notes) for the 2037 Notes (collectively, the “Par Call Dates”), the Issuers may redeem the applicable series of Notes, in whole or in part, at a price equal to the greater of (i) 100% of the principal amount of the Notes to be redeemed and (ii) the sum of the present values of the remaining scheduled payments of principal and interest to the applicable Par Call Date discounted to the applicable date of redemption (assuming the Notes matured on the applicable Par Call Date) on an annual basis at the Comparable Government Bond Rate (as defined in the Third Supplemental Indenture), plus 20 basis points in case of the 2034 Notes and 25 basis points in case of the 2037 Notes, plus, in each case, any accrued and unpaid interest thereon. The Issuers may redeem a series of Notes, in whole or in part, at any time and from time to time, on or after the applicable Par Call Date for such series of Notes at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to, but excluding, the date of redemption. 
If the Issuers experience specific kinds of changes of control, they will be required to offer to purchase each series of the Notes at a purchase price equal to 101% of the principal amount, plus accrued and unpaid interest. If holders of not less than 90% in aggregate principal amount of a series of Notes then outstanding validly tender and do not withdraw such Notes in an offer to purchase and the Issuers, or any third party making such an offer in lieu of the Issuers as described below, purchase all of such Notes properly tendered and not withdrawn by such Holders, the Issuers or such third party will have the right, upon not less than 10 days’ nor more than 60 days’ prior notice (provided that such notice (the “Second Change of Control Payment Date”) is given not more than 60 days following such repurchase pursuant to the offer to purchase described above) to redeem all Notes of such series that remain outstanding following such purchase on a date specified in such notice and at a price in cash equal to 101% of the aggregate principal amount of the Notes repurchased plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, on the Notes repurchased to, but excluding, the Second Change of Control Payment Date. 
The Notes will be senior unsecured obligations of the Issuers and will be guaranteed by the Company on a senior unsecured basis (the “Guarantee”). The Notes and the Guarantee will rank equal in right of payment with all of the Issuers’ and Company’s existing and future senior unsecured indebtedness, but will be effectively junior to all of the Issuers’ and the Company’s future secured indebtedness to the extent of the value of the assets securing such indebtedness and effectively junior in certain circumstances to indebtedness incurred under NXP B.V. and NXP Funding LLC’s Revolving Credit Facility with respect to certain assets of NXP B.V. and its subsidiaries in the event that such assets may secure such indebtedness in the future. The Notes and the Guarantee will rank senior in right of payment to the Issuers’ and the Company’s existing and future subordinated indebtedness and will be structurally subordinated to all of the liabilities, including trade payables, of their subsidiaries. 
The Indenture provides for customary events of default, including failure to make required payments; failure to comply with certain agreements or covenants; failure to pay, or acceleration of, certain other material indebtedness; certain events of bankruptcy and insolvency; and failure to pay certain judgments. An event of default under the Indenture will allow either the Trustee or the holders of at least 30% in aggregate principal amount of the then outstanding Notes of the applicable series to accelerate the amounts due under the Notes. 
The foregoing description of the Indenture does not purport to be a complete summary of the parties’ rights and obligations under the Indenture and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of the Indenture.  | Item 1.01
 | 
Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement. 
On November 25, 2026, American Tower Corporation (the “Company”) completed a registered public offering of €600.0 million aggregate principal amount of its 4.200% senior unsecured notes due 2031 (the “2031 notes”) and €600.0 million aggregate principal amount of its 4.500% senior unsecured notes due 2034 (the “2034 notes” and, together with the 2031 notes, the “Notes”), which resulted in aggregate net proceeds to the Company of approximately €1,191.3 million (approximately $1,317.0 million at the euro/U.S. dollar exchange rate of €1.00 = $1.1055, as reported by Bloomberg on November 12, 2026), after deducting commissions and estimated expenses. The Company intends to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, including but not limited to refinancing upcoming euro maturities. 
The Company issued the Notes under an indenture dated as of June 2, 2025 (the “Base Indenture”), between the Company and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by a supplemental indenture dated as of November 25, 2026 (the “Supplemental Indenture No. 4” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”), among the Company, the Trustee and U.S. Bank Europe DAC, UK Branch, as paying agent. The following description of the Indenture is a summary and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the detailed provisions of the Indenture. 
The 2031 notes will mature on February 20, 2031 and bear interest at a rate of 4.200% per annum. The 2034 notes will mature on February 20, 2034 and bear interest at a rate of 4.500% per annum. Accrued and unpaid interest on the Notes will be payable in euros in arrears on February 20 of each year, beginning on February 20, 2027. Interest on the Notes will accrue from November 25, 2026 and will be computed on the basis of the actual number of days in the period for which interest is being calculated and the actual number of days from and including the last date on which interest was paid on the Notes. The terms of the Indenture, among other things, limit (a) the Company’s ability to merge, consolidate or sell assets, and (b) the Company’s and its subsidiaries’ abilities to incur liens. These covenants are subject to a number of exceptions, including that the Company and its subsidiaries may incur liens on assets, mortgages or other liens securing indebtedness, provided the aggregate amount of indebtedness secured by such liens shall not exceed 3.5x Adjusted EBITDA as defined in the Indenture. 
The Company may redeem the Notes at any time, in whole or in part, at its election at the applicable redemption price. If the Company redeems (a) the 2031 notes prior to January 20, 2031, or (b) the 2034 notes prior to December 20, 2033, the Company shall pay a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed plus a make-whole premium, together with accrued interest to the redemption date. If the Company redeems (a) the 2031 notes on or after January 20, 2031, or (b) the 2034 notes on or after December 20, 2033, the Company shall pay a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Notes being redeemed plus accrued interest to the redemption date. In addition, if the Company undergoes a Change of Control and Ratings Decline, each as defined in the Indenture, the Company may be required to repurchase all of the Notes at a purchase price equal to 101% of the principal amount of the Notes, plus accrued and unpaid interest (including additional interest, if any), up to but not including the repurchase date. 
The Indenture provides that each of the following is an event of default (“Event of Default”): (i) default for 30 days in payment of any interest due with respect to the Notes; (ii) default in payment of principal or premium, if any, on the Notes when due, at maturity, upon any redemption, by declaration or otherwise; (iii) failure by the Company to comply with covenants in the Indenture or Notes for 90 days after receiving notice; and (iv) certain events of bankruptcy or insolvency with respect to the Company or any of its Significant Subsidiaries, as defined in the Indenture. If any Event of Default arising under clause (iv) above occurs, the principal amount and accrued and unpaid interest on all the outstanding Notes will become due and payable immediately without further action or notice. If any other Event of Default occurs and is continuing, the Trustee or the holders of at least 25% in principal amount of the then outstanding Notes may declare the entire principal amount on all the outstanding Notes to be due and payable immediately. 
The foregoing is only a summary of certain provisions and is qualified in its entirety by the terms of the Base Indenture, as filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “SEC”) on June 2, 2025 as an exhibit to the Company’s Registration Statement on Form S-3 (No. 333-287714), and the Supplemental Indenture No. 4, a copy of which is filed herewith as Exhibit 4.1, and incorporated by reference herein.

Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions 
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 
Federal Reserve Board 
For release at 3:00 p.m. EST 
 Share 
The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). 
By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. 
Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500. 
The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026. 
The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases.

PRESS RELEASE
ECB and Sveriges Riksbank conclude agreement for Sweden to join T2
25 November 2026
Agreement paves way for settlement of large-value payments in Swedish kronor using T2
Migration targeted for February 2030
The European Central Bank (ECB) and Sveriges Riksbank have concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem’s real-time gross settlement system. Today, ECB President Christine Lagarde and Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen took part in a signing ceremony for the T2 currency participation agreement at the ECB.
This agreement will enable Sveriges Riksbank to use T2 for settling large-value payments in Swedish kronor. Migration is targeted for February 2030.
Joining T2 will move Sweden’s large-value payment settlement from a national platform to shared European infrastructure. Sveriges Riksbank and Swedish financial institutions will benefit from investments in security, resilience and technological development that are shared across participating markets, as well as from common European standards. Payments will continue to be settled in Swedish kronor using central bank money.
“Shared payment infrastructure strengthens Europe’s strategic autonomy and supports a more integrated financial system,” said ECB President Christine Lagarde. “This agreement builds on our partnership with Sveriges Riksbank and our joint commitment to safe and efficient payments.”
“By connecting to the European T2 platform for settling payments in Swedish kronor, we can, together with the ECB and other central banks, ensure that the Swedish settlement system becomes an even safer and more efficient payment system in the long run, both in everyday life and in a crisis,” said Sveriges Riksbank Governor Erik Thedéen.
TARGET Services are the Eurosystem’s financial market infrastructure for settling large-value payments, instant payments and securities transactions, and for managing collateral. In addition to payments in euro, T2 already supports large-value payments in Danish kroner. Both Sweden and Denmark use TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS) to settle instant payments in Swedish kronor and Danish kroner respectively.
Photos of the signing ceremony will be available on the ECB’s multimedia portal.

CONSUMER PRICE INDEX - OCTOBER 2026
The Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) increased 0.4 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis in October 
after rising 0.6 percent in September, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. 
The index for shelter rose 0.3 percent in October, accounting for over thirty percent of the monthly all items increase. 
The food index increased 0.5 percent in October, as the food at home index rose 0.4 percent and the food away from home 
index increased 0.5 percent. The index for energy increased 0.7 percent over the month following a 5.2-percent increase 
in September. 
The index for all items less food and energy rose 0.3 percent in October, as it did in September and August. Indexes that 
increased over the month include recreation, medical care, motor vehicle insurance, household furnishings and operations, 
and education. Conversely, the index for used cars and trucks and the index for communication were among the small number 
of major indexes that decreased in October.

Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions.

 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - OCTOBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted, the 
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in 
September and 0.4 percent in August. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise 
since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 
0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent.
The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.5 percent in October, the 
same as in September. For the 12 months ended in October, prices for final demand less foods, 
energy, and trade services advanced 4.9 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent in October following 
a 2.5-percent rise in September. Over 60 percent of the advance in October is attributable to prices 
for final demand goods less foods and energy, which moved up 0.5 percent. The index for final 
demand foods increased 1.3 percent. In contrast, prices for final demand energy edged down 0.1 
percent. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 
percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022.
Product detail: Within the index for final demand goods in October, prices for basic organic 
chemicals advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes for fresh and dry vegetables; gas fuels; aeronautical, 
nautical, and navigational instruments; jet fuel; and processed young chickens also moved higher. 
(See table 2.) Conversely, diesel fuel prices fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for passenger 
cars also declined. 
Final demand services: The index for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent in October, the 
fifth consecutive advance. Three-fourths of the October rise can be traced to a 2.0-percent increase in 
prices for final demand transportation and warehousing services. The index for final demand services 
less trade, transportation, and warehousing advanced 0.2 percent. In contrast, margins for final 
demand trade services decreased 0.2 percent.
Product detail: Over 80 percent of the October increase in the index for final demand services is 
attributable to prices for truck transportation of freight, which rose 3.9 percent. The indexes for fuels 
and lubricants retailing; health, beauty, and optical goods retailing; food and alcohol wholesaling; 
hospital outpatient care; and traveler accommodation services also moved higher. Conversely, 
margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling fell 4.2 percent. Prices for system software 
publishing and for airline passenger services also declined.

For the 12 months ended in October, prices for processed goods for intermediate demand increased 
14.6 percent, the largest 12-month rise since jumping 17.2 percent in July 2022.
Product detail: More than 40 percent of the October advance in the index for processed goods for 
intermediate demand can be traced to prices for basic organic chemicals, which moved up 3.9

fabricated structural metal products, and prepared animal feeds also increased. Conversely, prices for

Unprocessed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate

Product detail: A major factor in the October decline in the index for unprocessed goods for

How does EIA compare different types of energy? 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review 
 Note: Btu=British thermal units 
To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren’t combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity. 
For combustible fuels, EIA uses thermal conversion factors to convert the physical units into heat content values. Because these factors can change based on the specific characteristics of fuels being produced at different points in time, we update our conversion factors each year. 
We publish heat content data for more than 30 petroleum products, 4 types of coal, and natural gas. Each fuel has a unique chemistry and heat content, and the heat content can vary based on the different types of fuel in the mix. For example, the heat content of anthracite coal is higher than the heat content of lignite. The aggregate heat content of coal generally varies based on the mix of the different types of coal produced and consumed. 
The aggregate heat contents for petroleum consumption and production have declined in recent decades because of decreasing use of residual fuel oil, which has relatively high heat content, and increasing use of fuels with a lower heat content—such as motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and hydrocarbon gas liquids. 
Our heat content estimates for natural gas have fluctuated within a relatively narrow range because of highly consistent pipeline specifications. Methane, the primary component of natural gas, has a heat content of 1,010 Btu per cubic foot. Other gases such as ethane, biomass gases, synthetic gases, and supplemental gases, which may be left in the natural gas stream, have higher heat content values. 
Total coal thermal conversion factors depend on the relative mix of coal types consumed and produced that year. Anthracite and bituminous coals have higher heat contents than lignite and subbituminous coals. Subbituminous coal production and consumption have increased over time, bringing down coal’s aggregate heat contents. 
To measure how efficient a power plant is at converting the fuel into electricity, we use heat rates. While thermal conversion factors measure the heat content of a fuel, heat rates measure the efficiency of power plants to convert fuel into heat and then into electricity. The heat rate is the amount of energy used to generate one kilowatthour (kWh) of electricity. The lower the heat rate, the higher the efficiency of a power plant to convert fuel into electricity. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review 
Since 2001—the earliest year in our data—heat rates for electricity generation from coal and petroleum have risen slightly, while the heat rate for electricity generation from natural gas has gone down, due in part to more efficient combined-cycle plants coming online. 
Power plants using nuclear energy and noncombustible renewables—such as hydro, wind, solar, and geothermal—generate electricity without burning fuel. For nuclear energy, EIA uses a measurement of the heat produced from nuclear fission in the reactor core. 
For noncombustible renewable energy, we use the captured energy approach. Captured energy is the energy available for consumption after converting a renewable resource into electricity, net of conversion losses. The captured energy approach uses the heat content of electricity, which is constant (3,412 Btu/kWh).

Almost 60% of primary energy used for electricity is lost to conversion and transmission 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Monthly Energy Review 
In 2025, the United States consumed 34 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) of primary energy to deliver 14 quads of electricity sales to end users, with nearly 60% lost. About 95% of the losses came from converting primary energy into electricity, mostly due to lost heat from burning coal and natural gas. The remaining 5% was lost in the course of delivering electricity across grid infrastructure to homes and businesses.
